build.checks: the model compiles; every #guard of the facts, counterexamples and examples holds; every proof is checked by Lean's kernel; the axiom audit passes
howChecked: lake build checks every proof. The build fails if any proof is wrong or missing.

The Audit library runs #assert_standard_axioms on every theorem named below (40 about TDH, 30 about P53). It fails the build unless the theorem depends only on Lean's three standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). A sorry fails it, and so does native_decide, which trusts the compiler.

Counterexamples and examples are checked at every build too. Some are theorems proved in the kernel by decide. The rest are #guard evaluations of the model, which trust Lean's compiler, as the checks of P26's stated numbers in Tdh/Facts.lean do.

sections.title: Netting invariance
sections.asked: Netting invariance (D131): the result depends only on each transaction's net movements; adding an out-and-back pair or reordering movements inside a transaction changes no output
sections.result: Proved for the stacks only, whenever both replays have a result, for transactions with one timestamp and one txHash (which §3.2 requires). False for the other values, a record's balance and raw included: §5's mint facts read the logged steps, so a mint and its burn inside one transaction can make a token eligible and give a wallet a balance it did not have (counterexample I), and can change rates and other holders' finals (counterexample H). A token's balance and raw stay the same while its eligibility does; that follows from §7.2's definitions and is not a theorem here. P26 §7.1 states the property for the stacks (1c69528). False for every value under the first rule (fe8e1fe): five counterexamples
sections.guarantees: What it guarantees. Every acquisition stack after the replay, a sink's included, is fixed by each transaction's net movements. The assumptions are exactly the theorems' hypotheses: both replays have a result (an inserted step can make the underflow test fail, below), every transaction has one timestamp and one txHash (P26 §3.2 requires it, and checkNetting checks it), and both replays use one registry and one cluster map (the clusters come from delegation events, which transfers do not change).
sections.limits: What is false: the values beyond the stacks (counterexamples H and I, Tdh/Proofs/Counterexamples.lean). §5's mint facts (firstMint, minted, G, Nc) count every mint as logged, before netting (P26 §5, vector 40). Meme 1 has 10 copies minted to A and Meme 2 has 5 minted to B; a transaction sends one copy of Meme 1 from A to C. Inserting ZERO -> X and X -> ZERO of 10 copies of Meme 1 into that transaction leaves every net(w) and every pair unchanged, so every stack is the same. But minted[1] rises from 10 to 20, H from 10 to 20, Meme 2's rate from 2.00 to 4.00, and B's final from 800 to 1,600 (the total from 1,710 to 2,510). Such a mint can also set an earlier firstMint, and change eligibility, n_memes and the seasons. Eligibility decides which tokens a record holds at all (§7.2), so it changes balances and raws too. Case I: Meme 2 has 3 copies minted to B ten days before T, and Meme 1 has 5 copies minted to A an hour before T, so Meme 1 is not eligible and A has no record. Inserting ZERO -> X and X -> ZERO of one copy of Meme 1 into the transaction of Meme 2's mint leaves every net(w), every pair and every stack unchanged, but Meme 1's firstMint moves to ten days before T. Meme 1 becomes eligible: A has a record with balance 5 (raw 0), H rises from 3 to 6, and B, who no longer holds a full set, goes from 32 to 60. So the property cannot be stated for computeCycle's values, a record's balance and raw included; what holds is the stack theorem above, and the values are functions of the stacks and of §5's results. For a token whose eligibility stays the same, its balance and raw are read from its stacks and T (tokenValues), so they stay the same; that is §7.2's definition, not a separate theorem. Also outside the property, as P26 says. The underflow test decides whether an input is valid, so an inserted step that spends a copy before it arrives makes the input invalid (vector 44). The theorems assume one timestamp and one txHash per transaction; P26 §3.2 makes any other input invalid, and the model checks it (checkNetting).

sections.title: Conservation
sections.asked: Conservation: stack size equals balance; balances never negative under valid inputs; copies held add up to minted minus burned
sections.result: First two proved, with and without netting. The third is false when a sink sends: what holds is held = copies from sinks minus copies to sinks
sections.limits: What is false. "Copies held add up to minted minus burned." A transfer from DEAD credits its recipient with a fresh copy and is not a mint (§3.4). Case G: one copy minted, one sent by DEAD, two held. The inflow counts transfers from every sink: mints from ZERO, and sends from DEAD. What it does not cover. A sink's stack is not a balance: sinks are credit-only. The ages in a stack do change with netting; that is netting's purpose.

sections.title: Totals and identity records
sections.asked: Totals: total TDH equals the sum of identity TDH, which equals the sum of wallet TDH
sections.result: The first holds by definition (computeCycle_totals restates how cycleTotals sums; with the 2^53 range). The second is false for finals: a counterexample. Proved instead: every identity's balance, raw and base, in total and per token, are the sums over its wallet records, and every wallet record belongs to exactly one identity
sections.limits: What is false. "The sum of identity TDH equals the sum of wallet TDH." An identity's boost is computed on its own holdings and each token's final is rounded once for the identity (§7.3, §8.4). Case F: two wallets of one identity each hold one Gradient for 100 days. Each wallet record has boost 1.02 and final 102; the identity has boost 1.04 and final 208. The total is 208, not 204. P26 §7.3 now says so, with this example.

sections.title: Order
sections.asked: Order: any permutation of the input list with the same canonical sort gives the same output
sections.result: Proved for the model's decoded inputs: any permutation of the transfers, of the delegation events and of the ignored logs' positions, including §3.1's position checks. Raw logs reach these lists through the decoder, which is outside the model
sections.guarantees: What it guarantees. The order in which the decoded items arrive in the model's input lists cannot matter. When two transfers share a canonical key, or two items of different logs share a (block, logIndex), an ignored log among them, the input is invalid (§3.1), and the error names the first clash in sorted order, which is the same for every order.
sections.limits: What it does not cover. The theorems are about decoded items. Raw logs reach them through the decoder, which is outside the model, so the order of raw logs is not covered: the runner's adapter is not proved, and when several raw logs are malformed, the one it reports can depend on their order. A transfer's position fields are part of the input: changing them changes the canonical order, as it should. The claims list (totalMax per Meme) is read as a map by Meme id.

sections.title: Liveness, the cap and the slices
sections.asked: P53 §6.3-§6.4: no capped party exceeds 19.99% of W; slices sum exactly
sections.result: Proved, and stronger: no party at all exceeds 19.99%; the loop stops within six passes, with at most five capped. The proof needs every party's accounts to keep a valid key, which P53 §6.2 now makes part of liveness; for live parties it holds with no assumption on keys. The keys left after the no-pool rule and the lease are inputs of the model, not proved, and the cap needs at least six parties of positive weight
sections.limits: What it does not cover. Membership of designated groups, the lease (the vote in N-7 to N) and key validity are inputs here; the no-pool rule is modelled only for the example. With fewer than six parties there is no cap (CAP_INACTIVE), and the theorems say nothing.

sections.title: Incidents and exclusions
sections.asked: P53 §13.1: no evidence shortens an exclusion in force; evidence for cycles before the end of an earlier exclusion never opens a new incident
sections.result: Proved for a node that keeps incident records, each with the step and length fixed when it opened, which P53 §13.1 now prescribes; pruning records on P53's schedule changes no exclusion. False for a node that recomputes incidents from the evidence it holds: a counterexample
sections.limits: What it does not cover. Joining nodes that read timing from certificates, differences between nodes' views, which account a fault belongs to, the attribution of a fault naming the current cycle "once that cycle's window closes" (the model lets a fault's proof cycle be any cycle at or after the one it names), and the voiding of votes.

sections.title: The acquisition stack
sections.limits: These theorems are about how the model stores a stack: they show that it behaves as P26 §7.1's list. Which entries the replay pushes and takes is the subject of sections 1 and 2.
sections.guarantees: The first proofs about the model. They show that the run-length stack of Tdh.Stack is exactly P26 §7.1's "ordered list of acquisition timestamps": push appends at the end, takeLast removes exactly the last amount entries and returns them in order, it fails exactly when the list is shorter (the input is then invalid), and size is the list's length. Everything the model computes from stacks therefore follows P26's list semantics.

theorems.statement: The order of a pass-through's legs. Identities {A, E} and {C, D}. A holds a copy acquired 100 days before T, D one acquired 90 days before. In one transaction 10 days before T, both send to a pass-through W, which forwards to C and E. The first rule paired in order of first appearance: in one order A with C and D with E (no age carries, total 20), in the other A with E and D with C (both carry, total 190). The current rule pairs in address order, A with C and D with E, for both.
theorems.doesNotGuarantee: A counterexample shows that the claim fails on one input. It proves nothing about other inputs, and says nothing about how often the claim fails.

theorems.statement: A burn and a forwarded mint, without any consolidation. A burns a copy while X passes a fresh mint to B, in one transaction. The first rule counted ZERO by its gross sends and receipts: in one order the pairs were ZERO -> B and A -> ZERO (ZERO credited with A's burn), in the other ZERO -> ZERO, which moves nothing, and A -> B. The current rule nets ZERO to zero in both: one pair, A -> B.

theorems.statement: Two sends, and an out-and-back appended. Identity {A, B}. A holds copies acquired 100 and 50 days before T. One transaction sends them to B one at a time. The first rule did not net it (no address both sent and received), so B's list ended with the older copy; an out-and-back B -> Y, Y -> B appended made it netted, and B's list ended with the newer copy. A later sale of one copy then left B the other: 50 or 100. The current rule nets every group: one pair A -> B of two copies, with or without the out-and-back.

theorems.claim: Copies held add up to minted minus burned
theorems.statement: Copies held are not minted minus burned. A transfer from DEAD credits its recipient with a fresh copy and is not a mint (§3.4). One Meme is minted to B, and DEAD sends a copy to A: two copies are held, one was minted, none was burned. What holds is held = inflow - outflow (held_eq_inflow_sub_outflow), where the inflow counts transfers from every sink: from ZERO and from DEAD.

theorems.claim: Steps that leave every net(w) unchanged change no value" (P26 §7.1 before 2026-10-15)
theorems.statement: A mint and its burn change values, with every net movement unchanged. Until 2026-10-15 P26 §7.1's property said that steps leaving every net(w) unchanged change no value. They change no stack (net_invariance), but §5's mint facts read the logged steps. Meme 1 has 10 copies minted to A and Meme 2 has 5 minted to B; a transaction sends one copy of Meme 1 from A to C. Inserting ZERO -> X and X -> ZERO of 10 copies of Meme 1 into that transaction leaves every net(w) and every pair unchanged, but minted[1] rises from 10 to 20, so H doubles, Meme 2's rate doubles from 2.00 to 4.00, and B's final goes from 800 to 1,600.

theorems.claim: Such steps change no stack, balance or raw" (P26 §7.1 after H, until round 3 of 2026-10-15)
theorems.statement: A mint and its burn change a balance, with every stack unchanged. After case H, P26 §7.1 said that such steps change no stack, balance or raw. Only the stacks are proved (replayHoldings_invariance): a record holds a token's balance and raw only while the token is eligible (§7.2, walletTokens), and eligibility reads §5's mint facts. Meme 2 has 3 copies minted to B ten days before T; Meme 1 has 5 copies minted to A an hour before T, so Meme 1 is not eligible and A has no record. Inserting ZERO -> X and X -> ZERO of one copy of Meme 1 into the transaction of Meme 2's mint leaves every net(w), every pair and so every stack as it was, but moves Meme 1's firstMint to ten days before T. Meme 1 becomes eligible: A has a record with balance 5 (raw 0, held under a day), H rises from 3 to 6, and B, who no longer holds a full set, goes from 32 to 60. P26 §7.1 gives this example since round 3 of 2026-10-15, and states the property for the stacks; a token's balance and raw stay the same only while its eligibility does.
